clue.text: Roman rustic deity shows fear at the fences

explanation.surface: A country god of ancient Rome loses his nerve when faced with a row of fences.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions in one clue, with 'at' as the link: Pales the Roman god of shepherds, the verb 'pales', and the noun 'pales', stakes that make a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: Pales was the Roman protector of flocks; someone who goes white with dread blanches; and the pointed stakes of a palisade are pales.

clue.text: Dog one classifies among. Boxers

parts.note: a pug is a small snub-nosed breed of dog
I is the Roman numeral for one
to list items is to classify them in order

explanation.surface: A dog breed is sorted among the boxers.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Boxers' another dog breed beside the pug; it means prizefighters.
explanation.definitionFit: Prizefighters who fight with their fists are pugilists.

clue.text: Premise. from problem mathematics

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of the words that follow

explanation.surface: An assumption drawn from a maths problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' takes the letters out of probLEM MAthematics.
explanation.definitionFit: In logic and mathematics a subsidiary proposition assumed or proved for use in a proof is a premise of the argument.

clue.text: Impressive work. of. some marine hunters

explanation.definitionFit: Pressing a seal into wax is impressing; the trade of men who hunt seals at sea is called by the same name.

clue.text: Heavenly toparch ?

parts.note: toparch, a petty ruler, splits as 'top arch': the vaulted arch at the very top of the sky

explanation.definitionFit: The vault of the heavens is pictured as a great arch spread over the earth.

clue.text: Tart with, for. example, raised projecting edge

parts.note: a flan is an open tart

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the letters are read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: A pastry with a lip raised up around its rim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns EG upwards in this down clue, giving GE after FLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A rim jutting out from a wheel or pipe, used for strength or attachment.

clue.text: Expedient tried, out to cure Rose

indicators.note: tried out suggests experimenting with arrangements, so the letters of the following words are reordered

explanation.surface: A remedy is tested to heal someone called Rose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tried out' rearranges CURE ROSE; 'to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A means of getting by in difficulty, an expedient, is something to fall back on.

clue.text: "The air broke' into a mist.. (Browning put his finger on it.?)

definitions.text: "The air broke' into a mist.. (Browning put his finger on it.?)

parts.words: "The air broke' into a mist.. (Browning put his finger on it.?)
parts.note: a line from Robert Browning's 'The Patriot' describing the air becoming a fine spray, and a finger pressed on a nozzle to release one

explanation.walkthrough: Browning's line is 'The air broke into a mist with bells'; a spray can turns liquid into a mist when a finger presses its button.
explanation.definitionFit: A pressurised can releases its contents as a fine spray of particles suspended in the air.

clue.text: Vacancy, do, we' hear, for a monster?:

indicators.note: asks whether the words that follow are heard rather than seen, signalling something spoken

parts.note: Loch Ness without its famous monster would be an empty Ness

explanation.surface: Asking whether we hear of a monster showing up for an empty post.
explanation.walkthrough: Loch Ness in Scotland is home to the legendary monster; with the monster gone it would be 'empty Ness', which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of being unfilled, a void or blank space, is a vacancy.

clue.text: Music for nine players rising to, join wood section

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a nonet is a composition for nine performers

explanation.surface: Musicians in a group of nine stand up to perform a piece in a carpentry workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns NONET upwards in this down clue; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In carpentry the projecting tongue cut on a piece of timber fits into a mortise to fix two pieces together.

clue.text: Radiation that turns mama's head in the Inn

indicators.note: in places the turned word within the name of the Inn

parts.note: Gray's Inn is one of London's four Inns of Court, where barristers train

indicators.note: turns says the first pair of letters of the word mama is flipped round
head limits the turning to the front of the word mama, its first two letters

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: Some radiation in a pub makes mother's head spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns ... head' flips only MA at the front of MAMA, giving AMMA, which goes inside GRAYS (Gray's Inn, a London Inn of Court for barristers) after its G.
explanation.definitionFit: These are very high-energy electromagnetic waves, a form of radiation given off by radioactive decay.

clue.text: Rhode Island bird to reach maturity

parts.note: RI is the standard abbreviation for the US state of Rhode Island
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A bird from Rhode Island grows up.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is the PEN, the female swan, not the Rhode Island Red hen the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that matures becomes fully ready, the same process of coming to full growth.

clue.text: Who is to go first ?

parts.note: read as a query about who will lead the way: a question about taking the lead

explanation.definitionFit: A loaded query worded to push a witness towards a particular reply; the clue's question is literally about who leads.

clue.text: Poet one needs to' cultivate ?

explanation.definitionFit: Richard Savage was an 18th-century English poet, friend of Samuel Johnson; an uncivilised barbarian is someone society would need to refine and educate.

clue.text: Greatly respected, even mistakenly overvalued

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece above the second
mistakenly says the word even is written wrongly, its letters in a jumbled order

parts.note: rated means valued or assessed

explanation.surface: Highly esteemed, though wrongly overrated.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs 'over' and 'valued' together as overrated; split them, so 'over' sets VENE (from 'even', jumbled by 'mistakenly') above RATED in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Something held in deep reverence or honour is greatly respected.

clue.text: Where oarsmen do the washing-up ?

parts.note: rowers who pull a pair of oars are scullers, so the room where they wash dishes is named after them

explanation.definitionFit: The back kitchen room where dishes and pans were washed in older houses.

clue.text: OK boys, are they corrected?$ asks the publisher

definitions.text: OK boys, are they corrected?$ asks the publisher

indicators.note: corrected implies the letters were wrong and are put right by rearranging them

explanation.surface: A publisher checks with his staff whether the proofs have been fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corrected' rearranges OK BOYS ARE; the whole clue is the publisher's question about the annual books he issues.
explanation.definitionFit: Annual publications summarising a year's events, the kind a publisher would issue and check each year.

clue.text: Composer has a saying that bears fruit

parts.note: Alban Berg was an Austrian composer
a mot is a witty saying, from French

explanation.surface: A composer has a proverb about fruitfulness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' joins the pieces. The bergamot tree is a citrus tree whose fruit gives oil used to flavour Earl Grey tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A citrus tree producing pear-shaped fruits whose rind gives a fragrant oil.

clue.text: Look out man for crab

explanation.definitionFit: A guard on watch is a lookout; the sentinel crab is an Indo-Pacific crab with long eyestalks that stand up like a watchman.

clue.text: One ship's. officer holds it for take off

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: holds means the officer contains the next word within him

parts.note: a mate is a merchant ship's officer below the captain

explanation.surface: One officer on board a ship keeps hold of something for the launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take off' means to mimic, not to depart as the ship surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To take someone off is to mimic them, copying their manner.

clue.text: Shame the old army girls are recalled from holiday

parts.note: fie is an old exclamation of shame or disgust

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters for the old army girls run backwards

parts.note: the ATS, the Auxiliary Territorial Service, was the British women's army in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Disgraceful: the former women soldiers are called back from their leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are recalled' turns ATS into STA. The ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service) was the women's branch of the British Army from 1938 to 1949.
explanation.definitionFit: A festival day of celebration, especially in Spain or Latin America, is a public holiday.

clue.text: At home, with Jane' near the coast

parts.note: in means at home
Jane Shore was the mistress of King Edward IV of England

explanation.surface: Indoors with Jane, close to the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the pieces. Jane Shore, mistress of Edward IV, is the subject of Nicholas Rowe's 1714 play 'Jane Shore'.
explanation.definitionFit: Close to the shoreline, as fishing done in coastal waters.

clue.text: Donnish chap ? We are right

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right; that the full run of letters also reads straight through the printed words is a coincidence of this charade, not a hidden word

explanation.surface: Asking about a scholarly fellow, and insisting that we are correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Donnish' looks like 'like a university don'; it means 'one who dons', puts on clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To don is to put on clothes, so the person who puts them on is the one clothing is on.

clue.text: Male rendezvous at which, wild women slung brick

indicators.note: wild suggests the following words are thrown about out of control, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bar for men where furious women hurled a brick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' shuffles WOMEN SLUNG BRICK. A working men's club is a British social club, traditionally for male manual workers.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a social club was traditionally a gathering place for male labourers to drink and meet.

clue.text: Jester returned for a bet

parts.note: a wag is a joker or jester

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the short word for 'for' is read backwards

parts.note: re means as regards or concerning, close to 'for' in the sense of 'about'

explanation.surface: A clown comes back to place a bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns RE (concerning, standing in for 'for') into ER after WAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A stake placed on an outcome, a gamble, is a bet.

clue.text: Big shareholders have their pride.

parts.note: the biggest share of anything is the '... share', and these big cats live in groups called prides

explanation.definitionFit: Big cats that live in family groups called prides and take the largest share, as in the phrase 'lion's share'.

clue.text: Almanachsburg

parts.note: a coined word: the German '-burg' (town) of the famous Almanach, the directory of European royalty and nobility

explanation.walkthrough: The Almanach de Gotha was a directory of European royalty, first published in the German town of Gotha in 1763.
explanation.definitionFit: This town in Thuringia gave its name to the almanac of royalty and nobility published there.

clue.text: Did this traveller spoil the company game ?.

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil it
polo is a game played on horseback with mallets

explanation.surface: A question about whether an explorer wrecked a party's sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Did' and 'the' only join; the surface's 'company game' points to a party game, here split into company and game.
explanation.definitionFit: The Venetian merchant who journeyed to China in the 13th century is history's most famous traveller to the East.

clue.text: The compiler blushes for this Irish dog !

parts.note: someone who blushes goes red
the setter is the person who compiles the crossword

explanation.surface: The crossword maker goes pink over a breed of Irish hound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The compiler' is the setter of the puzzle; 'for this' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish setter, with its rich chestnut coat, is a breed of gundog from Ireland.

clue.text: Letters once collared by Lancastrians

parts.note: the collar of livery worn by supporters of the House of Lancaster was made of linked S-shaped letters

explanation.walkthrough: The 'collar of SS' was the livery collar of the House of Lancaster in medieval England, a chain of linked S shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural name for the nineteenth letter of the alphabet, the shape linked in that Lancastrian collar.
